claim: Conceptual metaphors are linguistic constructions.
source: Conceptual metaphors are linguistic constructions.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract without supporting evidence in the manuscript itself.

claim: Humans mentally represent social rank as a pyramidal-like structure.
source: Such a metaphor is humans' mental representation of social rank as a pyramidal-like structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bosserman (1983) later in the manuscript and represents established knowledge.

claim: High-ranked individuals are represented in higher positions than low-ranked individuals in humans.
source: High-ranked individuals are represented in higher positions than low-ranked individuals.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the manuscript (Bosserman, 1983; Saunders, 1989; Weber, 1991; Maslow, 1943) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Conceptual metaphorical mapping between social rank and the representational domain exists in chimpanzees.
source: We show that conceptual metaphorical mapping between social rank and the representational domain exists in our closest evolutionary relatives, the chimpanzees.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing modulation of response latencies.

claim: A high-ranked individual presented in the higher position and a low-ranked individual in the lower position led to quicker identity discrimination than a high-ranked individual in the lower and a low-ranked individual in the higher position in chimpanzees.
source: We found a modulation of response latencies by the rank of the presented individual and the position on the display: a high-ranked individual presented in the higher and a low-ranked individual in the lower position led to quicker identity discrimination than a high-ranked individual in the lower and a low-ranked individual in the higher position.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the experimental data presented in the Results section and Figure 1.

claim: A spatial representation of dominance hierarchy in chimpanzees suggests that a natural tendency to systematically map an abstract dimension exists in the common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees.
source: Such a spatial representation of dominance hierarchy in chimpanzees suggests that a natural tendency to systematically map an abstract dimension exists in the common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about chimpanzees and evolutionary relationships.

claim: Expressions linking high/low spatial positions with high/low status are widely observed across cultures and languages.
source: "high" vs "low status", "top of the heap", "bottom of the barrel": These or similar expressions are widely observed across cultures and languages (Pinker, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pinker (1997).

claim: The cross-modal correspondence between the visuospatial domain (high or low) and an abstract domain (rank) has been described as a conceptual metaphor.
source: The cross-modal correspondence between the visuospatial domain (high or low) and an abstract domain (rank) has been described as a conceptual metaphor (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980a, b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lakoff and Johnson (1980a, b).

claim: Conceptual metaphors have been thought to be uniquely human.
source: The cross-modal correspondence between the visuospatial domain (high or low) and an abstract domain (rank) has been described as a conceptual metaphor (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980a, b) and thought to be uniquely human (Feldman and Narayanan, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Feldman and Narayanan (2004).

claim: A conceptual metaphor takes one concept and connects that to another concept in order to better understand that concept.
source: A conceptual metaphor takes one concept and connects that to another concept in order to better understand that concept.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established knowledge about conceptual metaphors.

claim: The way we think and act is largely influenced by conceptual metaphors, even without being fully aware of them.
source: The way we think and act is largely influenced by conceptual metaphors, even without being fully aware of them (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lakoff and Johnson (1980a).

claim: Neural representations of objects and entities exist in monkeys.
source: Decades of research have shown that neural representations of objects and entities exist in monkeys (Sigala et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sigala et al. (2002).

claim: Neural representations of objects and entities exist in apes.
source: Decades of research have shown that neural representations of objects and entities exist in monkeys (Sigala et al., 2002), apes (Fukushima et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fukushima et al. (2010).

claim: Neural representations of objects and entities exist in humans.
source: Decades of research have shown that neural representations of objects and entities exist in monkeys (Sigala et al., 2002), apes (Fukushima et al., 2010) and humans (Kourtzi and Kanwisher, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kourtzi and Kanwisher (2001).

claim: The abilities of object representation and recognition apply to recognition of faces.
source: The abilities of object representation and recognition further apply to social domains such as recognition of faces (Dahl et al., 2007; Dahl et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dahl et al. (2007) and Dahl et al. (2013).

claim: The abilities of object representation and recognition apply to recognition of conspecifics.
source: The abilities of object representation and recognition further apply to social domains such as recognition of faces (Dahl et al., 2007; Dahl et al., 2013), conspecifics (Dahl et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dahl et al. (2007).

claim: The abilities of object representation and recognition apply to recognition of ingroup-outgroup members.
source: The abilities of object representation and recognition further apply to social domains such as recognition of faces (Dahl et al., 2007; Dahl et al., 2013), conspecifics (Dahl et al., 2007), and ingroup-outgroup members (Pokorny and de Waal, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pokorny and de Waal (2009).

claim: A crucial skill for living in social groups is to express one's status and to recognize the status of others via visual or vocal cues.
source: To avoid or reduce costly social conflicts among individuals, a crucial skill for living in social groups is to express one's status and to recognize the status of the others via visual or vocal cues (Paxton et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Paxton et al. (2010).

claim: Recognition of status or rank allows inferences about expected roles of oneself and of others during group situations.
source: Recognition of status or rank allows inferences about expected roles of oneself and of others during group situations (Ridgeway and Diekema, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ridgeway and Diekema (1989).

claim: Access to food resources, information and social respect are facilitated with high rank in the hierarchy.
source: Access to food resources, information and social respect are facilitated with high rank in the hierarchy, while some degree of protection and care are granted to lower-ranked individuals (Fiske, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fiske (1992).

claim: Some degree of protection and care are granted to lower-ranked individuals.
source: Access to food resources, information and social respect are facilitated with high rank in the hierarchy, while some degree of protection and care are granted to lower-ranked individuals (Fiske, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fiske (1992).

claim: In many non-human species, spatial information such as perceived physical body size and facial and body postures serve as an indicator of social status.
source: In many non-human species, spatial information, such as perceived physical body size, and facial and body postures, serve as an indicator of social status (Maestripieri, 1996; Tiedens and Fragale, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maestripieri (1996) and Tiedens and Fragale (2003).

claim: Humans developed a conceptual metaphor which connects social rank to the spatial domain.
source: Besides these non-verbal cues, we humans developed a conceptual metaphor, which connects social rank to the spatial domain (e.g., "high" vs "low status" [Pinker, 1997]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pinker (1997) and represents established knowledge.

claim: Humans represent social status in a pyramidal-like structure.
source: Accordingly, humans represent social status in a pyramidal-like structure (Bosserman, 1983)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bosserman (1983).

claim: High-ranked individuals are represented in spatially higher positions than low-ranked individuals in diverse contexts including stratification.
source: high-ranked individuals are represented in spatially higher positions than low-ranked individuals in diverse contexts, for example, stratification (Saunders, 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Saunders (1989).

claim: High-ranked individuals are represented in spatially higher positions than low-ranked individuals in organizations.
source: high-ranked individuals are represented in spatially higher positions than low-ranked individuals in diverse contexts, for example, stratification (Saunders, 1989), organizations (Weber, 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weber (1991).

claim: High-ranked individuals are represented in spatially higher positions than low-ranked individuals in the context of human needs.
source: high-ranked individuals are represented in spatially higher positions than low-ranked individuals in diverse contexts, for example, stratification (Saunders, 1989), organizations (Weber, 1991), religion, family, human needs (Maslow, 1943)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maslow (1943).

claim: There was a main effect for coherence on response latencies (F(2, 30) = 5, m.s.e. = 1.10e+004, p<0.001).
source: Using a mixed model ANOVA with coherence and position as fixed factors, we found a main effect for coherence (F(2, 30) = 5, m.s.e. = 1.10e+004, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no main effect for position on response latencies (p>0.34).
source: Using a mixed model ANOVA with coherence and position as fixed factors, we found a main effect for coherence (F(2, 30) = 5, m.s.e. = 1.10e+004, p<0.001), but not for position (p>0.34)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no interaction effect between coherence and position on response latencies (p>0.83).
source: Using a mixed model ANOVA with coherence and position as fixed factors, we found a main effect for coherence (F(2, 30) = 5, m.s.e. = 1.10e+004, p<0.001), but not for position (p>0.34) or the interaction between the two factors (p>0.83)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was a significant response facilitation for coherent as opposed to incoherent trials (t(10) = -3.20, m.s.e. = 8.60e+003, p<0.01).
source: Post-hoc t-tests (Bonferroni-corrected for multiple comparisons) revealed a significant response facilitation for coherent as opposed to incoherent trials (t(10) = -3.20, m.s.e. = 8.60e+003, p<0.01 [one-tailed])
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was a significant response facilitation for coherent as opposed to close trials (t(10) = −1.92, m.s.e. = 1.14e+004, p<0.05).
source: Post-hoc t-tests (Bonferroni-corrected for multiple comparisons) revealed a significant response facilitation for coherent as opposed to incoherent trials (t(10) = -3.20, m.s.e. = 8.60e+003, p<0.01 [one-tailed]) and close trials (t(10) = −1.92, m.s.e. = 1.14e+004, p<0.05 [one-tailed]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no significant deterioration for incoherent compared to close trials (p>0.11).
source: However, there was no significant deterioration for incoherent compared to close trials (p>0.11)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There were significant deviations from zero for the high position (t(5) = 16.64, m.s.e. = 1.11e+004, p<0.001).
source: We found significant deviations from zero for the high position (t(5) = 16.64, m.s.e. = 1.11e+004, p<0.001 [one-tailed])
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There were significant deviations from zero for the low position (t(5) = 20.13, m.s.e. = 6.88e+003, p<0.001).
source: We found significant deviations from zero for the high position (t(5) = 16.64, m.s.e. = 1.11e+004, p<0.001 [one-tailed]) and for the low position (t(5) = 20.13, m.s.e. = 6.88e+003, p<0.001 [one-tailed])
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference between the positions high and low (p>0.55).
source: Further, there was no significant difference between the positions high and low (p>0.55).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: High-ranked participants showed the same response patterns as low-ranked participants.
source: High-ranked participants showed the same response patterns as low-ranked participants (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: None of the frequency distributions of response latencies were statistically different across the two participant groups (all p>0.54).
source: Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests revealed that none of the frequency distributions of response latencies were statistically different across the two participant groups (all p>0.54).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There is more variance in the responses of the low-ranked participants than the high-ranked participants.
source: As indicated in Figure 1D,E, there is more variance in the responses of the low-ranked (Figure 1E, four participants) than the high-ranked participants (Figure 1D, two participants)
evidence: This claim is supported by visual inspection of Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Low-ranked participants have lower sensitivity than high-ranked participants (t(14) = 2.53, m.s.e. = 8.36e+003, p<0.05).
source: there is more variance in the responses of the low-ranked (Figure 1E, four participants) than the high-ranked participants (Figure 1D, two participants), leading to a lower sensitivity in low-ranked participants (t(14) = 2.53, m.s.e. = 8.36e+003, p<0.05, Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: All stimuli elicited sensitivity scores in accordance with the hypothesis that coherent stimulus arrangements led to response facilitation and incoherent stimulus arrangements led to response deterioration.
source: Importantly, all stimuli elicited sensitivity scores in accordance with the hypothesis, that is, coherent stimulus arrangements led to response facilitation and incoherent stimulus arrangements led to response deterioration, indicated by positive values.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sensitivity index data presented in Figure 1H.

claim: In chimpanzees, discrimination performances between familiar conspecific faces are systematically modulated by the location and the social status of the presented individuals.
source: We showed that in chimpanzees discrimination performances between familiar conspecific faces are systematically modulated by the location and the social status of the presented individuals, leading to discrimination facilitation or deterioration.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings supported by the data presented in the Results section.

claim: Coherent arrangements as opposed to incoherent arrangements led to a facilitation of recognition in chimpanzees.
source: Coherent arrangements as opposed to incoherent arrangements led to a facilitation of recognition.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings supported by the data presented in the Results section.

claim: A high-ranked individual at the higher position and a low-ranked individual at the lower position caused recognition facilitation equivalently in chimpanzees.
source: Further, both, a high-ranked individual at the higher position and a low-ranked individual at the lower position caused recognition facilitation equivalently.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings supported by the data presented in the Results section.

claim: The participants were not trained on discriminating the ranks of the presented individuals.
source: Importantly, the participants were not trained on discriminating the ranks of the presented individuals.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and procedure.

claim: The participants were substantially affected by the rank while discriminating the identity of individuals.
source: Instead, they were substantially affected by the rank while discriminating the identity of those individuals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing modulation of response latencies by rank.

claim: The modulations are in accordance with a spatial arrangement representing high-ranked individuals at the top and low-ranked individuals at the bottom.
source: The modulations are in accordance with a spatial arrangement representing high-ranked individuals at the top and low-ranked individuals at the bottom, hence reflecting the inverse function of response latencies and spatial distance of two individuals on the display and in the mental hierarchy space of the participants.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: A confound between perceptual and conceptual determinants might exist.
source: It has to be noted that a confound between perceptual and conceptual determinants might exist.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging a potential limitation of the study.

claim: There might be a co-dependence of the perceptual and conceptual domains, with the conceptual domain having been established on the basis of the perceptual domain.
source: There might be a co-dependence of the two domains, with the conceptual domain having been established on the basis of the perceptual domain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the relationship between perceptual and conceptual domains.

claim: Response characteristics are similar in high-ranked and low-ranked participants.
source: Response characteristics are similar in high-ranked and low-ranked participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figures 1D and 1E and the statistical analyses.

claim: The effect is not merely based on perceptual cues but on, to some extent, conceptual components.
source: Thus, even though perceptual determinants cannot be fully excluded with this control, it is still suggestive that the effect is not merely based on perceptual cues but on, to some extent, conceptual components.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity of response characteristics across high-ranked and low-ranked participants.

claim: Individual stimuli elicited a comparable effect within and across stimulus sets.
source: We showed that individual stimuli elicited a comparable effect within and across stimulus sets by estimating sensitivity indices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sensitivity index analysis presented in Figure 1H.

claim: The two stimulus sets contributed equally to the effect.
source: In other words, the two stimulus sets contributed equally to the effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sensitivity index analysis.

claim: In humans, responses to low-digit numbers are faster with a left-side button-press whereas higher digits are categorized faster when right-side button-presses are required.
source: A spatial component of representation has been shown in other domains: for example in humans' responses to low-digit numbers are faster with a left-side button-press whereas higher digits are categorized faster when right-side button-presses are required (Dehaene et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dehaene et al. (1993).

claim: Merely looking at number causes a shift of attention to the left or the right side in humans.
source: Moreover, merely looking at number causes a shift of attention to the left or the right side (Fischer et al, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fischer et al. (2003).

claim: The mental number line reflects a cross-modal mapping of visual cues (numbers) and cognitive labels (values).
source: In other words, the mental number line reflects a cross-modal mapping of visual cues (numbers) and cognitive labels (values).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cited research on the mental number line.

claim: Social status and number comparisons recruit to some extent overlapping neural substrates in the intraparietal sulci of the human brain.
source: Interestingly, social status and number comparisons recruit to some extent overlapping neural substrates in the intraparietal sulci of the human brain (Chiao et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chiao et al. (2009).

claim: There is evidence for a non-verbal, supramodal neural representation of numerosity in the macaque ventral intraparietal sulcus and lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: There is evidence for a non-verbal, supramodal neural representation of numerosity in the macaque ventral intraparietal sulcus and lateral prefrontal cortex (Nieder, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nieder (2012).

claim: Neural evidence for cross-modal correspondences is missing.
source: however, neural evidence for cross-modal correspondences is missing.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Rare evidence for non-human cross-modal correspondences comes from visuo-auditory mappings between high luminance and high pitch in chimpanzees.
source: Rare evidence for non-human cross-modal correspondences comes from visuo-auditory mappings between high luminance and high pitch in chimpanzees (Ludwig et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ludwig et al. (2011).

claim: The relationship between luminance and pitch illustrates a form of sound-symbolism.
source: This relationship between luminance and pitch illustrates a form of sound-symbolism, which refers to the concept that in human language words and referents are not arbitrary (Nuckolls, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nuckolls (1999).

claim: The systematic mapping between luminance and pitch in chimpanzees suggests the emergence of an early vocabulary of human language.
source: Hence, while the existence of such a systematic mapping between luminance and pitch in chimpanzee suggests the emergence of an early vocabulary of human language (Ramachandran and Hubbard, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ramachandran and Hubbard (2001) and represents an inference about language evolution.

claim: The current study expands the finding of cross-modal correspondence in chimpanzees to a cross-modal correspondence between vision and an abstract domain: the social status.
source: we here expand this finding to a cross-modal correspondence between vision and an abstract domain: the social status.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the current study based on the experimental findings.

claim: A natural tendency to systematically map an abstract dimension in chimpanzees suggests that this tendency had already evolved in the common ancestors of humans and chimpanzees.
source: A natural tendency to systematically map an abstract dimension, such as social status, in our closest and nonlinguistic relatives, the chimpanzees, suggests that this tendency had already evolved in the common ancestors of humans and chimpanzees.
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary history based on the experimental findings in chimpanzees.

claim: This tendency might have influenced the emergence of metaphorical linguistics.
source: This tendency might have influenced the emergence of metaphorical linguistics, thinking via image schema, an embodied pre-linguistic structure of experience that motivates conceptual metaphor mappings (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980a).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the evolutionary origins of metaphorical linguistics, supported by citation to Lakoff and Johnson (1980a).

claim: Image schema is an embodied pre-linguistic structure of experience that motivates conceptual metaphor mappings.
source: thinking via image schema, an embodied pre-linguistic structure of experience that motivates conceptual metaphor mappings (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lakoff and Johnson (1980a).

claim: Orientational metaphors such as 'more is up', 'good is up' and 'dominant is up' are based on observational correlation between increasing a substance and seeing the level of the substance rise.
source: According to Lakoff (Lakoff and Johnson, 1980b), orientational metaphors, such as 'more is up', 'good is up' and 'dominant is up', are based on observational correlation between increasing a substance and seeing the level of the substance rise, like adding an element to a pile.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lakoff and Johnson (1980b).

claim: Orientational metaphors are good candidates for universal concepts given their strong physical basis.
source: Given the strong physical basis, these metaphors are good candidate for universal concepts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical basis of orientational metaphors.

claim: Until now, conceptual metaphors have been exclusive human experiences.
source: Until now, conceptual metaphors have been exclusive human experiences.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: The findings point in a different direction from conceptual metaphors being exclusively human.
source: Our findings point in a different direction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing conceptual metaphorical mapping in chimpanzees.

claim: Six chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes; 1 male juvenile, 2 female juveniles and 3 female adults) participated in this study.
source: Six chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes; 1 male juvenile, 2 female juveniles [both around 11 years] and 3 female adults [both around 31 years]) participated in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: The chimpanzees live in groups of 14 individuals with access to environmentally enriched outdoor (770 m2) as well as indoor compounds.
source: The chimpanzees live in groups of 14 individuals with access to environmentally enriched outdoor (770 m2) as well as indoor compounds.
evidence: This is a description of the housing conditions of the study participants.

claim: The chimpanzees participated in a variety of computer-controlled tasks in the past.
source: The chimpanzees participated in a variety of computer-controlled tasks in the past (Matsuzawa, 2003; Matsuzawa et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matsuzawa (2003) and Matsuzawa et al. (2006).

claim: The chimpanzees are experienced in horizontally aligned delayed matching-to-sample (DMS) tasks.
source: They are experienced in horizontally aligned delayed matching-to-sample (DMS) tasks
evidence: This is a description of the prior experience of the study participants.

claim: The chimpanzees are inexperienced in a vertical version of a DMS task.
source: however, they are inexperienced in a vertical version of a DMS task.
evidence: This is a description of the prior experience of the study participants.

claim: Effects of training in the vertically aligned DMS task can be ruled out.
source: Effects of training in the vertically aligned DMS task can be ruled out.
evidence: This is an inference based on the participants' inexperience with the vertical DMS task.

claim: The agreement of twenty independent raters on the social ranks of the chimpanzees was found to be Kappa = 1.00 (p<0.001), 95% CI (1.00, 1.00).
source: The agreement of twenty independent raters (researchers and caretakers familiar with the chimpanzees at the Primate Research Institute) on the social ranks of the chimpanzees was found to be Kappa = 1.00 (p<0.001), 95% CI (1.00, 1.00).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the inter-rater reliability analysis.

claim: Only correct trials went into the analyses, which is 69% (±4.5% S.E.M.) of all trials.
source: Only correct trials went into the analyses, which is 69% (±4.5% S.E.M.) of all trials.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis procedure and the accuracy rate.

claim: Chimpanzee participants were requested to discriminate face identities in a vertical arrangement.
source: Chimpanzee participants were requested to discriminate face identities in a vertical arrangement.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: A cue (individual 1, 750 ms) was sequentially presented followed by an inter-stimulus interval (500 ms) and two vertically arranged stimuli (match: individual 1; distractor: individual 2).
source: We sequentially presented a cue (individual 1, 750 ms) followed by an inter-stimulus interval (500 ms) and two vertically arranged stimuli (match: individual 1; distractor: individual 2) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The chimpanzees were required to indicate which of the two simultaneously presented faces corresponds to the initially presented face in identity by touching one of the faces.
source: The chimpanzees were required to indicate which of the two simultaneously presented faces (match, distractor) corresponds to the initially presented face (cue) in identity by touching one of the faces.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: The participants did not classify the stimuli based on social rank.
source: Note that the participants did not classify the stimuli based on social rank.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task design.

claim: The experiment included a neutral condition combining two pictures of closely ranked individuals in a trial (close condition).
source: In addition to coherent and incoherent combinations of stimulus and position, we included a neutral condition combining two pictures of closely ranked individuals in a trial (close condition).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.
